questions.question: Explain why South Africa is described as a water-scarce country.
questions.expected_answer: Average rainfall about 450-500 mm, roughly half the world average (about 860 mm); rainfall is unevenly distributed (over 1000 mm in parts of the east, under 200 mm in the west); unreliable, with droughts (e.g. El Nino 1992, 2015-16) and floods; high evaporation means only about 9% of rainfall becomes runoff; no very large rivers by world standards and many non-perennial rivers in the west.

questions.question: Describe the sources of water in South Africa.
questions.expected_answer: Surface water from rivers and dams (about 77%) - over 5000 large dams, e.g. Gariep and Vanderkloof (Orange), Sterkfontein; groundwater (about 9%) from aquifers via boreholes, vital for small towns and rural areas in the dry west and north; return flows and reuse of treated waste water (e.g. Beaufort West); desalination in some coastal towns; rainwater harvesting; imported water from Lesotho.

questions.question: What are inter-basin transfers, and how can South Africa close the gap between water supply and demand?
questions.expected_answer: Transfers move water from one river basin to another via tunnels, pipelines and canals, e.g. Lesotho Highlands Water Project (Katse Dam 1997, to the Vaal for Gauteng; royalties and hydro-electricity for Lesotho; relocation and corruption costs), Tugela-Vaal, Orange-Fish River Tunnel (1975), Western Cape Water Supply System. Closing the gap: increase supply (new dams such as Polihali, careful groundwater use, desalination, reuse, clearing alien plants) and reduce demand (fix leaks, efficient irrigation, water-saving devices, restrictions and tariffs, education - Cape Town halved use); protect water quality.
